kandidaty.zagolovok: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite
kandidaty.tekst:
sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite

This additional SQLite tool has been around for a while now - it was added as "experimental" in SQLite 3.47.0 in October 2024 and enhanced in SQLite 3.50.0 in May 2025. It was only today that I understood one of its most attractive characteristics.

Normally, if you want to grab a snapshot copy of a SQLite database, you need to use either the backup API or VACUUM INTO. In both cases you need enough disk space to create a duplicate copy of your database, so if you're on a small instance and you already use more than half of the available disk you are plain out of luck.

sqlite3_rsync can copy a snapshot of your database over an SSH connection to another machine, without first needing to create a full local copy!

It's also good for synchronizing an existing copy of a database without re-transmitting the entire thing over the network. It works in a similar way to regular rsync:

The core idea behind the protocol is that the replica sends cryptographic hashes for pages or groups of pages over to the origin side. The origin sends back page content that differs, or requests finer-grain hashes if a multi-page hash does not match. If the origin and replica start out being vastly different, the total network bandwidth can exceed the size of the entire database, due to the overhead of exchanging hashes, but the excess bandwidth is not great - a few percent at most.

Update: Hah! Turns out I wrote about this application of sqlite_rsync back in October 2024 when the tool was first released.

Tags: backups, sqlite

kandidaty.zagolovok: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
kandidaty.tekst:
My comment on The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features — Hacker News.

I had a NYT photographer take my picture at my home earlier this year (for a story about Moltbook, oddly enough). At one point I asked if they could fix things up if I had a stain on my shirt and they said absolutely not - they present photographs as they were taken, with cropping and balancing applied but no edits beyond that.

He did spend a bunch of time trying to find the best possible natural lighting for the shots he wanted.

The photo at the top of https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/02/technology/moltbook-ai-so... is my laptop, taken in my garden, after hunting around for the best spot that didn't have too much glare on the screen. You can see how dirty my screen is, too!

Photography for a newspaper is photo journalism, and they take it seriously.

(Thankfully I did not have a visible stain on my shirt.)

kandidaty.zagolovok: I asked Claude to populate a Civilization-style game map with real data from the US. Opus 5.5 downloaded and parse a ton
kandidaty.tekst:
@karpathy: I asked Claude to populate a Civilization-style game map with real data from the US. Opus 5.5 downloaded and parse a ton of public data and 7 hours and 45K lines of code later... it works :)

- 31 real data sources including Census, BEA, BLS, EIA, NOAA, USGS, DoD, NPS, FAA, FEMA, CDC...
- Real elevation, land cover, GDP, jobs, power plants, mines, ports, airports, bases, parks, universities, freight flows, disasters; all reconciled onto one 25 km hex grid.
- The data is converted into Civilization language, e.g. Gold yield is GDP. A city's districts are its real industry specializations: San Jose gets a Campus, Detroit is "Motor city". Its citizens are its real workforce: 1 in 4 San Jose workers are engineers, coders or scientists, against 1 in 14 nationally. Wonders are chosen by published rules, such as national parks by visitor numbers and universities by R&D spending, etc etc.
- 19 lenses (income, degrees, faith, disasters…), a City View for 524 metros, and nine advisors plus an Explorer. The Explorer turns any column for any of 3,100+ counties into a table and scatter plot, linked to the map.
- Claude decided to skip a few states and territories sry
- Built using Claude Code desktop app, Opus 5.5 on medium and turning on ultracode.

It's deployed here: https://karpathy.ai/usaciv/ and the "?" has the source link too. I don't exactly know where I was going with this but it's really fun to browse and play with. Possibly it can be expanded or built into a game. I only have half of my weekly Claude quote left though so someone else will have to take over :D. Claude also made a trailer:

Цитирует @wadefoster: Refounding Zapier means answering a lot of hard questions.

Like: "Why use Zapier, when Claude connects to my apps?"

The short answer: use them together. Your agent does the thinking. Zapier MCP plugs it into 10,000+ apps so it can take real actions in the tools you need.

@Zapier is for work that repeats: a new lead, a payment notification, the Monday morning report, anything that has to keep running after you close the chat.

Sure, you can set that up as a scheduled task in Claude, ChatGPT, etc. But then you're paying for AI tokens every time it wakes up to check for work, even when it finds nothing. 

Zapier’s AI Workflow Index priced 2,944 real workflows and found that 𝘀𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗹𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗻 𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝟮.𝟭𝘅 𝗮𝘀 𝗺𝘂𝗰𝗵 𝗮𝘀 𝗭𝗮𝗽𝘀.

A Zap starts when something actually happens. It runs the same steps every time and only calls AI for the parts that need judgment.

A scheduled task works great while you're at your computer. But who fixes it when it breaks at 2am? If you built it yourself, you do. If it's hosted on Zapier, Zapier fixes it on its own. Plus, when it sees you using AI for something simple automation or code could do? It recommends a fix. (Something the big labs aren’t enticed to do…)

The new Zapier works with whatever AI agent you already use. So use them together.

The next time you ask Claude or ChatGPT or Grok or Muse for the same thing twice, have it build a Zap.
